title: Two studies of a changing town
paragraphs: Passage A — The night-market sound map

A student team studied how noise moved through the night market. They recorded at the same six locations at 6 p.m., 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. for four Fridays. Fixed places and times made comparisons possible even when crowd size changed.

The first map was provisional because a festival had filled one street with performers. After an ordinary Friday produced a different pattern, the team marked both conditions rather than discarding either result. The council later used the map to place a quiet waiting area away from loudspeaker stalls.
As a child, Suri disliked the old clocktower bell because it interrupted conversations in the square. Years later, the mechanism failed, and the square felt strangely unfinished at each hour.

Suri played a phone recording of the bell, but its thin sound lacked the vibration she remembered feeling through the pavement. She realised that the bell had not merely announced time; it had connected people through a sound they experienced together.
When repairs restored the bell, Suri still found it loud. Yet she now heard it with affection, understanding that familiar sounds can become part of a place's shared memory.
